mcqs.q: Pigmentation of the oral mucosa is defined as:
opts: Discoloration due to accumulation of pigments
mcqs.explain: Pigmentation = discoloration of the oral mucosa/gingiva due to accumulation of pigments.

mcqs.q: Which factor does NOT normally determine the colour of oral mucosa?
mcqs.explain: Mucosal colour depends on keratinization, melanocytes and vascularization — not the plaque score.

mcqs.q: A brown oral pigmentation is most likely due to:
mcqs.explain: Brown = melanin; blue/purple = vascular or deep melanin; grey/black = metal such as amalgam.

mcqs.q: A grey/black gingival pigmentation near a restoration most likely represents:
mcqs.explain: Grey/black macular pigment from silver compounds = amalgam tattoo (often near restorations).

mcqs.q: Physiologic (racial) pigmentation classically appears as:
mcqs.explain: Racial melanosis is diffuse, symmetric brown pigmentation of the attached/facial gingiva.

mcqs.q: Aesthetic treatment of racial gingival pigmentation includes:
mcqs.explain: Depigmentation by gingivectomy or laser is used when treatment is desired for esthetics.

mcqs.q: The proposed mechanism of smoker's melanosis is that a tobacco component:
mcqs.explain: A component of tobacco smoke stimulates melanocytes; hormones and heat also contribute.

mcqs.q: The most common oral mucosal lesion of melanocytic origin is the:
mcqs.explain: The oral melanotic macule (an 'intraoral freckle') is the most common melanocytic oral lesion.

mcqs.q: A typical oral melanotic macule is:
opts: Homogeneous brown, < 1 cm, on lip or anterior gingiva
mcqs.explain: It is a homogeneous, well-defined brown macule under 1 cm, commonly on the lower lip or anterior maxillary gingiva.

mcqs.q: The oral melanotic macule is caused by:
opts: Increased melanin in the basal cell layer
mcqs.explain: It results from increased production/deposition of melanin in the basal cell layer.

mcqs.q: Multiple perioral and labial melanotic macules with intestinal polyposis suggest:
mcqs.explain: Peutz-Jeghers = autosomal-dominant intestinal polyposis with perioral/labial pigmented macules (pathognomonic).

mcqs.q: Café-au-lait macules characteristically have:
opts: Irregular margins and a brown colour
mcqs.explain: Café-au-lait macules are brown patches with irregular margins, present at or soon after birth.

mcqs.q: Café-au-lait macules are a feature of McCune-Albright syndrome, which also includes:
mcqs.explain: McCune-Albright = polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, endocrinopathies and soft-tissue myxomas.

mcqs.q: Neurofibromatosis type 1 is suspected when a post-pubertal patient has:
mcqs.explain: ≥6 café-au-lait macules >1.5 cm (post-pubertal) or >0.5 cm (pre-pubertal) raise suspicion of NF1.

mcqs.q: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is inherited as:
mcqs.explain: Peutz-Jeghers is an autosomal-dominant condition.

mcqs.q: In Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, which finding is pathognomonic?
mcqs.explain: Lip and perioral pigmented macules are pathognomonic of Peutz-Jeghers.

mcqs.q: An amalgam tattoo is best described as:
opts: An iatrogenic deposition of amalgam in the mucosa
mcqs.explain: It is iatrogenic — amalgam transferred to the mucosa during restoration; soluble silver gives the colour.

mcqs.q: A large amalgam tattoo may be distinguished radiographically because it is:
mcqs.explain: If large enough, amalgam particles are radio-opaque on a radiograph — a helpful clue.

mcqs.q: Drug-induced oral melanosis (e.g. from minocycline or antimalarials) typically:
opts: Is flat and fades months after stopping the drug
mcqs.explain: Drug-induced lesions are flat (non-nodular) and tend to fade within months of discontinuing the drug.

mcqs.q: Post-inflammatory oral hyperpigmentation is classically associated with:
mcqs.explain: Post-inflammatory pigmentation follows prior injury/inflammation and is seen in lichen planus.

mcqs.q: The most common intraoral site for a melanocytic nevus is the:
mcqs.explain: Oral melanocytic nevi are uncommon and most often occur on the hard palate.

mcqs.q: Oral melanocytic nevi most often present in patients:
mcqs.explain: They are usually seen in patients younger than 40 and are mostly asymptomatic.

mcqs.q: Which nevus carries the highest rate of malignant transformation?
mcqs.explain: In the junctional nevus, cells cross the junction and 'drop off' into connective tissue — high malignant-transformation risk.

mcqs.q: The blue colour of a blue nevus is due to:
opts: Spindle melanocytes deep in the connective tissue
mcqs.explain: Deeply placed spindle-shaped melanocytes scatter light to give a blue clinical colour.

mcqs.q: A hemangioma is fundamentally:
opts: A benign vascular tumour of proliferating endothelium
mcqs.explain: A hemangioma is a benign vascular tumour formed by endothelial-cell proliferation.

mcqs.q: Diascopy (the blanching test) is used to identify a lesion that is:
mcqs.explain: Vascular lesions blanch on pressure (positive diascopy); melanin/metal pigment does not.

mcqs.q: A varix differs from a hemangioma in that it is:
opts: An acquired focal venous dilatation, not a true tumour
mcqs.explain: A varix is an acquired focal dilatation of a vein from loss of wall elasticity — not a true neoplasm.

mcqs.q: Lingual varices are most typically found on the:
mcqs.explain: 'Lingual varices' classically appear as bluish dilated veins on the ventral tongue.

mcqs.q: A key clinical risk of an oral hemangioma during dental treatment is:
mcqs.explain: Because they are vascular, hemangiomas can bleed significantly during extractions or surgery.

mcqs.q: Identify the lower-lip lesion shown.
mcqs.explain: A solitary, well-defined homogeneous brown macule of the lower lip is a typical oral melanotic macule.

mcqs.q: This pattern of perioral and intraoral macules points to which syndrome?
mcqs.explain: Perioral freckle-like macules with intraoral pigmentation are pathognomonic of Peutz-Jeghers.

mcqs.q: Identify the bluish lesions on the ventral tongue.
mcqs.explain: Dilated bluish veins on the ventral tongue that blanch on pressure are lingual varices.

saqs.q: Define oral pigmentation and list the three factors that determine the colour of oral mucosa.
saqs.a: Pigmentation = discoloration of the mucosa from pigment accumulation. Colour depends on keratinization, melanocyte number/activity, and vascularization.

saqs.q: Classify pigmented oral lesions into three groups with one example of each.
saqs.a:
1. Melanin — melanotic macule
2. Vascular — hemangioma / varix
3. Exogenous/metal — amalgam tattoo

saqs.q: Contrast a hemangioma and a varix (nature and one clinical point).
saqs.a:
HemangiomaVarix
Naturebenign vascular tumouracquired venous dilatation
Notemay involuteventral tongue, elderly
Both blanch on diascopy.

saqs.q: A 30-year-old has a <1 cm brown macule on the lower lip plus similar macules on the perioral skin, hands and feet. Diagnosis and inheritance?
saqs.a: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome — autosomal dominant, with intestinal polyposis.

saqs.q: Why is the junctional nevus clinically significant?
saqs.a: Its junctional activity (cells dropping into connective tissue) carries a high rate of malignant transformation.

saqs.q: A soft bluish compressible tongue swelling blanches on pressure. Diagnosis and one dental risk?
saqs.a: Hemangioma (vascular, positive diascopy). Risk: significant bleeding during extraction/surgery.
